claim: South Africa experienced three VOC pandemic waves (Beta, Delta, and Omicron BA.1) by February 2022.
source: here we apply a model-inference system to reconstruct SARS-CoV-2 transmission dynamics in South Africa, a country that has experienced three VOC pandemic waves (i.e. Beta, Delta, and Omicron BA.1) by February 2022.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is based on the data analyzed in the study covering March 2020 to February 2022.

claim: The model-inference system accounts for changing detection rates, infection seasonality, nonpharmaceutical interventions, and vaccination.
source: We estimate key epidemiologic quantities in each of the nine South African provinces during March 2020 to February 2022, while accounting for changing detection rates, infection seasonality, nonpharmaceutical interventions, and vaccination.
evidence: The methodology section describes these components as part of the model-inference system design.

claim: Model estimated underlying infection rates are in line with independent epidemiological data and investigations.
source: Model validation shows that estimated underlying infection rates and key parameters (e.g. infection-detection rate and infection-fatality risk) are in line with independent epidemiological data and investigations.
evidence: The validation is demonstrated through comparisons with serology, hospitalization, and excess mortality data as shown in Figure 1B and Appendix 1—figure 2.

claim: Retrospective predictions capture pandemic trajectories beyond the model training period.
source: In addition, retrospective predictions capture pandemic trajectories beyond the model training period.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2 and Appendix 1—figure 3, showing predictions made 1-2 weeks before case peaks.

claim: South Africa had the earliest surge for Beta and Omicron VOCs.
source: However, South Africa is also unique in that the country had the earliest surge for two of the five VOCs identified to date – namely, Beta (Tegally et al., 2021) and Omicron (Viana et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies documenting the early detection of these variants in South Africa.

claim: The model-inference system is able to fit weekly case and death data in each of the nine South African provinces.
source: Overall, the model-inference system is able to fit weekly case and death data in each of the nine South African provinces (Figure 1A, Appendix 1—figure 1, and additional discussion in Appendix 1).
evidence: Figure 1A shows the model fit to observed case and death data across all provinces.

claim: Model estimated cumulative infection rates roughly match corresponding serology measures and trends over time.
source: Compared to seroprevalence measures taken at multiple time points in each province, our model estimated cumulative infection rates roughly match corresponding serology measures and trends over time; as expected, model estimates were higher than serology measures taken during later months (Figure 1B).
evidence: Figure 1B shows the comparison between model estimates and independent seroprevalence data from multiple surveys.

claim: Model estimated infection numbers were well correlated with numbers of hospitalizations for all four pandemic waves (r>0.75).
source: Second, compared to hospital admission data, across the nine provinces, model estimated infection numbers were well correlated with numbers of hospitalizations for all four pandemic waves caused by the ancestral, Beta, Delta, and Omicron (BA.1) variants, respectively (r>0.75, Appendix 1—figure 2A–D).
evidence: The correlation analysis with independent hospitalization data validates the model estimates.

claim: Model-estimated infection numbers were correlated with age-adjusted excess mortality for both the ancestral and Delta wave (r=0.86 and 0.61, respectively).
source: Third, model-estimated infection numbers were correlated with age-adjusted excess mortality for both the ancestral and Delta wave (r=0.86 and 0.61, respectively; Appendix 1—figure 2A and C).
evidence: The correlation with independent excess mortality data provides validation of model estimates.

claim: For the Omicron (BA.1) wave, mortality rates decoupled from infection rates due to prior infection and/or vaccination.
source: For the Omicron (BA.1) wave, like many other places, due to prior infection and/or vaccination (Nyberg et al., 2022; Wolter et al., 2022), mortality rates decoupled from infection rates (Appendix 1—figure 2D).
evidence: This observation is supported by citations to studies showing reduced severity with Omicron and is consistent with data shown in Appendix 1—figure 2D.

claim: The model was able to accurately predict the remaining trajectories of cases and deaths in most of the nine provinces for both the Delta and Omicron (BA.1) waves, 1–2 weeks before the case peak.
source: Despite these challenges, 1–2 weeks before the case peak and 3–5 weeks before the observed death peak, the model was able to accurately predict the remaining trajectories of cases and deaths in most of the nine provinces for both the Delta and Omicron (BA.1) waves (Figure 2 for the four most populous provinces and Appendix 1—figure 3 for the remainder).
evidence: Figure 2 and Appendix 1—figure 3 show the retrospective predictions compared to observed data.

claim: The estimated infection-detection rate during the first pandemic wave in Gauteng was 4.59% (95% CI: 2.62–9.77%).
source: For Gauteng, the estimated infection-detection rate during the first pandemic wave was 4.59% (95% CI: 2.62–9.77%), and increased slightly to 6.18% (95% CI: 3.29–11.11%) and 6.27% (95% CI: 3.44–12.39%) during the Beta and Delta waves, respectively (Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: This is a model-inference estimate based on fitting case and death data while accounting for under-detection.

claim: A population-level sero-survey in Gauteng found 68.4% seropositivity among those unvaccinated at the end of the Delta wave.
source: In particular, a population-level sero-survey in Gauteng found 68.4% seropositivity among those unvaccinated at the end of the Delta wave (Madhi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited from an independent seroprevalence study.

claim: 32.83% (95% CI: 15.42–57.59%) of the population in Gauteng were infected during the first wave.
source: Using our inferred under-detection (Figure 3E), we estimate that 32.83% (95% CI: 15.42–57.59%, Appendix 1—table 2) of the population in Gauteng were infected during the first wave, predominantly during winter when more conducive climate conditions and relaxed public health restrictions existed (see the estimated seasonal and mobility trends, Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a model-inference estimate based on the infection-detection rate and observed cases, shown in Figure 3 and Appendix 1—table 2.

claim: Serology measures taken in Gauteng at the end of the first wave ranged from 15% to 27% among 6 sero-surveys during November 2020.
source: This high infection rate, while with uncertainty, is in line with serology measures taken in Gauteng at the end of the first wave (ranging from 15% to 27% among 6 sero-surveys during November 2020; Figure 1B)
evidence: This is based on independent seroprevalence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A study showed 30% sero-positivity among participants enrolled in the Novavax NVX-CoV2373 vaccine phase 2a-b trial in South Africa during August – November 2020.
source: and a study showing 30% sero-positivity among participants enrolled in the Novavax NVX-CoV2373 vaccine phase 2a-b trial in South Africa during August – November 2020 (Shinde et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from an independent vaccine trial study.

claim: 21.87% (95% CI: 12.16–41.13%) of the population in Gauteng were infected during the Beta wave.
source: With the emergence of Beta, another 21.87% (95% CI: 12.16–41.13%) of the population in Gauteng – including reinfections – is estimated to have been infected, even though the Beta wave occurred during summer under less conducive climate conditions for transmission (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a model-inference estimate shown in the context of Figure 3A.

claim: Beta likely substantially eroded prior immunity, consistent with laboratory studies showing low neutralizing ability of convalescent sera against Beta.
source: This dramatic increase in population susceptibility (vs. a likely more gradual change due to waning immunity), to the then predominant Beta variant, suggests Beta likely substantially eroded prior immunity and is consistent with laboratory studies showing low neutralizing ability of convalescent sera against Beta (Garcia-Beltran et al., 2021; Wall et al., 2021).
evidence: This inference is based on model estimates of population susceptibility changes and is supported by citations to laboratory studies.

claim: An increase in transmissibility is evident for Beta, after accounting for concurrent NPIs and infection seasonality.
source: In addition, an increase in transmissibility is also evident for Beta, after accounting for concurrent NPIs and infection seasonality (Figure 3C; note transmissibility is computed as the product of the estimated variant-specific transmission rate and the infectious period; see Materials and methods for detail).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C based on model-inference estimates.

claim: The estimated overall infection-fatality risk for Beta was about twice as high as the ancestral SARS-CoV-2 (0.19% vs. 0.09%).
source: Further, consistent with in-depth epidemiological findings (Abu-Raddad et al., 2021a), the estimated overall infection-fatality risk for Beta was about twice as high as the ancestral SARS-CoV-2 (0.19% [95% CI: 0.10–0.33%] vs. 0.09% [95% CI: 0.05–0.20%], Figure 3F and Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: This is a model-inference estimate shown in Figure 3F and Appendix 1—table 3, consistent with cited epidemiological findings.

claim: The model-inference system estimates a 49.82% (95% CI: 25.22–90.79%) attack rate by Delta in Gauteng.
source: The model-inference system estimates a 49.82% (95% CI: 25.22–90.79%) attack rate by Delta, despite the large number of infections during the previous two waves.
evidence: This is a model-inference estimate based on the data and model parameters.

claim: Delta has high transmissibility, as reported in multiple studies.
source: This large attack rate was possible due to the high transmissibility of Delta, as reported in multiple studies (Public Health England, 2021; Allen et al., 2022; Challen et al., 2021; Earnest et al., 2021; Vöhringer et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies reporting Delta's high transmissibility.

claim: Delta has immune erosive properties relative to both the ancestral and Beta variants.
source: and the immune erosive properties of Delta relative to both the ancestral and Beta variants (Dhar et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021; de Oliveira and Lessells, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing Delta's immune evasion properties.

claim: Prior to the detection of Omicron (BA.1) in Gauteng, estimated cumulative infection numbers surpassed the population size.
source: Due to these large pandemic waves, prior to the detection of Omicron (BA.1) in Gauteng, estimated cumulative infection numbers surpassed the population size (Figure 4B), indicating the large majority of the population had been infected and some more than once.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B based on model-inference estimates of cumulative infections.

claim: With the rise of Omicron (BA.1), the model-inference system estimates a very large increase in population susceptibility.
source: With the rise of Omicron (BA.1), the model-inference system estimates a very large increase in population susceptibility (Figure 3D), as well as an increase in transmissibility (Figure 3C)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D and 3C based on model-inference estimates.

claim: The Omicron (BA.1) wave progresses much more quickly than previous waves, peaking 2–3 weeks after initiating marked exponential growth.
source: however, unlike previous waves, the Omicron (BA.1) wave progresses much more quickly, peaking 2–3 weeks after initiating marked exponential growth.
evidence: This is observed from the data and model estimates of the Omicron wave dynamics.

claim: By the end of February 2022, the model-inference system estimates a 44.49% (95% CI: 19.01–75.30%) attack rate during the Omicron (BA.1) wave in Gauteng.
source: By the end of February 2022, the model-inference system estimates a 44.49% (95% CI: 19.01–75.30%) attack rate, with only 4.26% (95% CI: 2.46–9.72%) of infections detected as cases, during the Omicron (BA.1) wave in Gauteng.
evidence: This is a model-inference estimate based on the data through February 2022.

claim: Estimated overall infection-fatality risk during the Omicron (BA.1) wave was about 30% of that during the Delta wave in Gauteng (0.03% vs. 0.11%).
source: In addition, consistent with the reported 0.3 odds of severe disease compared to Delta infections (Wolter et al., 2022), estimated overall infection-fatality risk during the Omicron (BA.1) wave was about 30% of that during the Delta wave in Gauteng (0.03% [95% CI: 0.02–0.06%] vs. 0.11% [95% CI: 0.06–0.21%], based on documented COVID-19 deaths; Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: This is a model-inference estimate consistent with cited studies on Omicron severity.

claim: Estimated average cumulative infections across the nine provinces ranged from 60% of the population in Limpopo to 122% in Northern Cape before the Omicron (BA.1) wave.
source: Overall, all nine provinces likely experienced three large pandemic waves prior to the growth of Omicron (BA.1); estimated average cumulative infections ranged from 60% of the population in Limpopo to 122% in Northern Cape (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B based on model-inference estimates across provinces.

claim: Excess mortality before the Omicron (BA.1) wave was as high as 0.47% of the South African population by the end of November 2021.
source: Excess mortality before the Omicron (BA.1) wave was as high as 0.47% of the South African population by the end of November 2021 (The South African Medical Research Council (SAMRC), 2021)
evidence: This is cited from an independent excess mortality report.

claim: South Africa has a relatively young population with a median age of 27.6 years.
source: despite the relatively young population (median age: 27.6 years (Anonymous, 2020b) vs. 38.5 years in the US [United States Census Bureau, 2020])
evidence: This is cited demographic data comparing South Africa to the US.

claim: Beta eroded immunity among 63.4% (95% CI: 45.0–77.9%) of individuals with prior ancestral SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: In the above context, we estimate that Beta eroded immunity among 63.4% (95% CI: 45.0–77.9%) of individuals with prior ancestral SARS-CoV-2 infection and was 34.3% (95% CI: 20.5–48.2%) more transmissible than the ancestral SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is a model-inference estimate based on changes in population susceptibility during the Beta wave.

claim: Beta was 34.3% (95% CI: 20.5–48.2%) more transmissible than the ancestral SARS-CoV-2.
source: In the above context, we estimate that Beta eroded immunity among 63.4% (95% CI: 45.0–77.9%) of individuals with prior ancestral SARS-CoV-2 infection and was 34.3% (95% CI: 20.5–48.2%) more transmissible than the ancestral SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is a model-inference estimate shown in Table 1 and Figure 4D.

claim: Estimates for Beta immune erosion and transmissibility are consistent across the nine provinces.
source: These estimates for Beta are consistent across the nine provinces (Figure 4D, 1st column and Table 1), as well as with our previous estimates using national data for South Africa (Yang and Shaman, 2021c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D and Table 1, and is consistent with previous work cited.

claim: Recoverees of ancestral SARS-CoV-2 infection in the Novavax trial had a similar likelihood of COVID-19 (mostly due to Beta) compared to those seronegative at enrollment.
source: Additional support for the high immune erosion of Beta is evident from recoverees of ancestral SARS-CoV-2 infection who were enrolled in the Novavax NVX-CoV2373 vaccine phase 2a-b trial (Shinde et al., 2021) and found to have a similar likelihood of COVID-19, mostly due to Beta, compared to those seronegative at enrollment.
evidence: This is cited from the Novavax vaccine trial study.

claim: Delta eroded 24.5% (95% CI: 0–53.2%) of prior immunity gained from infection by ancestral SARS-CoV-2 and/or Beta, and/or vaccination.
source: Overall, we estimate that Delta eroded 24.5% (95% CI: 0–53.2%) of prior immunity (gained from infection by ancestral SARS-CoV-2 and/or Beta, and/or vaccination) and was 47.5% (95% CI: 28.4–69.4%) more transmissible than the ancestral SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is a model-inference estimate based on changes in population susceptibility during the Delta wave.

claim: Delta was 47.5% (95% CI: 28.4–69.4%) more transmissible than the ancestral SARS-CoV-2.
source: Overall, we estimate that Delta eroded 24.5% (95% CI: 0–53.2%) of prior immunity (gained from infection by ancestral SARS-CoV-2 and/or Beta, and/or vaccination) and was 47.5% (95% CI: 28.4–69.4%) more transmissible than the ancestral SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is a model-inference estimate shown in Table 1 and Figure 4D.

claim: Studies have reported a 27.5% reinfection rate during the Delta pandemic wave in Delhi, India.
source: Consistent with this finding, and in particular the estimated immune erosion, studies have reported a 27.5% reinfection rate during the Delta pandemic wave in Delhi, India (Dhar et al., 2021)
evidence: This is cited from a study on reinfection rates in Delhi.

claim: Studies have reported reduced ability of sera from Beta-infection recoverees to neutralize Delta.
source: and reduced ability of sera from Beta-infection recoverees to neutralize Delta (Liu et al., 2021; de Oliveira and Lessells, 2021).
evidence: This is cited from studies on neutralization capacity against Delta.

claim: Omicron (BA.1) is 94.0% (95% CI: 73.5–121.5%) more transmissible than the ancestral SARS-CoV-2.
source: Overall, we estimate that Omicron (BA.1) is 94.0% (95% CI: 73.5–121.5%) more transmissible than the ancestral SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is a model-inference estimate shown in Table 1 and Figure 4D.

claim: The estimated transmissibility of Omicron (BA.1) is higher than Delta and consistent with in vitro and/or ex vivo studies showing Omicron (BA.1) replicates faster within host than Delta.
source: This estimated transmissibility is higher than Delta and consistent with in vitro and/or ex vivo studies showing Omicron (BA.1) replicates faster within host than Delta (Garcia-Beltran et al., 2022; Hui et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on model estimates and is consistent with cited laboratory studies.

claim: Omicron (BA.1) eroded 54.1% (95% CI: 35.8–70.1%) of immunity due to all prior infections and vaccination.
source: In addition, we estimate that Omicron (BA.1) eroded 54.1% (95% CI: 35.8–70.1%) of immunity due to all prior infections and vaccination.
evidence: This is a model-inference estimate based on changes in population susceptibility during the Omicron wave.

claim: Studies have reported low neutralization ability of convalescent sera from infections by all previous variants against Omicron (BA.1).
source: Supporting the suggestion of broad-spectrum immune erosion of Omicron (BA.1), studies have reported low neutralization ability of convalescent sera from infections by all previous variants (Rössler et al., 2022; Cele et al., 2022)
evidence: This is cited from studies on neutralization capacity against Omicron.

claim: Studies have reported high attack rates among vaccinees in several Omicron (BA.1) outbreaks.
source: as well as high attack rates among vaccinees in several Omicron (BA.1) outbreaks (Brandal et al., 2021; Helmsdal et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited from studies on Omicron outbreaks among vaccinated populations.

claim: The Delta variant caused a third large pandemic wave in South Africa that resulted in 0.2% excess mortality.
source: This is evident from the large Delta wave in South Africa, which resulted in 0.2% excess mortality (vs. 0.08% during the first wave and 0.19% during the Beta wave [The South African Medical Research Council (SAMRC), 2021]).
evidence: This is cited from excess mortality data.

claim: Omicron BA.4/BA.5 subvariants have been shown to evade prior immunity including from BA.1 infection.
source: More recently, due to the Omicron BA.4/BA.5 subvariants that have been shown to evade prior immunity including from BA.1 infection (Cao et al., 2022; Khan et al., 2022)
evidence: This is cited from studies on BA.4/BA.5 immune evasion.

claim: A fifth wave began in South Africa during May 2022, leading to increases in both cases and hospitalizations.
source: a fifth wave began in South Africa during May 2022, leading to increases in both cases and hospitalizations (Sarah et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited from a report on the fifth wave.

claim: Multiple SARS-CoV-2 VOCs/VOIs have emerged in the two years since pandemic inception.
source: Third, multiple SARS-CoV-2 VOCs/VOIs have emerged in the two years since pandemic inception.
evidence: This is established knowledge based on global surveillance data.

claim: Except for the Alpha variant, the other four important VOCs (Beta, Gamma, Delta, and Omicron) all produced some level of immune erosion.
source: Indeed, except for the Alpha variant, the other four important VOCs (i.e. Beta, Gamma, Delta, and Omicron) all produced some level of immune erosion.
evidence: This is inferred from the model estimates and cited literature on variant characteristics.

claim: Later VOCs, like Delta and Omicron, appear to have been more genetically distinct from previous variants.
source: In addition, later VOCs, like Delta and Omicron, appear to have been more genetically distinct from previous variants (van der Straten et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited from a study on genetic distinctiveness of variants.

claim: Development of a universal vaccine that can effectively block SARS-CoV-2 infection in addition to preventing severe disease is urgently needed.
source: Given this pattern, to prepare for future antigenic changes from new variants, development of a universal vaccine that can effectively block SARS-CoV-2 infection in addition to preventing severe disease (e.g. shown in Mao et al., 2022) is urgently needed (Morens et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings and is supported by citations to relevant studies.

claim: The model uses an SEIRSV (susceptible-exposed-infectious-recovered-susceptible-vaccination) construct.
source: The epidemic model follows an SEIRSV (susceptible-exposed-infectious-recovered-susceptible-vaccination) construct per Equation 1:
evidence: This describes the mathematical structure of the epidemic model used in the study.

claim: The seasonality function assumes that humidity has a bimodal effect on seasonal risk of infection, with both low and high humidity conditions favoring transmission.
source: In essence, the seasonality function in Equation 2 assumes that humidity has a bimodal effect on seasonal risk of infection, with both low and high humidity conditions favoring transmission [i.e. the parabola in 1st set of brackets, where q(t) is weekly specific humidity measured by local weather stations]
evidence: This describes the assumptions built into the seasonality model component.

claim: The seasonality effect is further modulated by temperature, with low temperatures promoting transmission and temperatures above a certain threshold limiting transmission.
source: and this effect is further modulated by temperature, with low temperatures promoting transmission and temperatures above a certain threshold limiting transmission [i.e. 2nd set of brackets, where T(t) is weekly temperature measured by local weather stations and Tc is the threshold].
evidence: This describes the temperature component of the seasonality model.

claim: The inference system uses the ensemble adjustment Kalman filter (EAKF), a Bayesian statistical method.
source: The inference system uses the ensemble adjustment Kalman filter (EAKF [Anderson, 2001]), a Bayesian statistical method, to estimate model state variables (i.e. S, E, I, R from Equation 1) and parameters
evidence: This describes the statistical method used for parameter estimation, with citation to the original method.

claim: The EAKF uses an ensemble of 500 model realizations.
source: Briefly, the EAKF uses an ensemble of model realizations (n=500 here), each with initial parameters and variables randomly drawn from a prior range (see Appendix 1—table 5).
evidence: This describes the specific implementation of the EAKF in this study.

claim: Provincial level COVID-19 case, mortality, and vaccination data were sourced from the Coronavirus COVID-19 (2019-nCoV) Data Repository for South Africa (COVID19ZA).
source: Provincial level COVID-19 case, mortality, and vaccination data were sourced from the Coronavirus COVID-19 (2019-nCoV) Data Repository for South Africa (COVID19ZA)(Data Science for Social Impact Research Group at University of Pretoria, 2021).
evidence: This describes the data source for the primary epidemiological data used in the study.

claim: Hourly surface station temperature and relative humidity came from the Integrated Surface Dataset (ISD) maintained by NOAA.
source: Hourly surface station temperature and relative humidity came from the Integrated Surface Dataset (ISD) maintained by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and are accessible using the 'stationaRy' R package (Iannone, 2020a; Iannone, 2020b).
evidence: This describes the data source for weather data used in the seasonality model.

claim: Mobility data were derived from Google Community Mobility Reports.
source: Mobility data were derived from Google Community Mobility Reports (Google Inc, 2020); we aggregated all business-related categories (i.e. retail and recreational, transit stations, and workplaces) in all locations in each province to weekly intervals.
evidence: This describes the data source for mobility data used to represent NPIs.

claim: Model-inference was initiated the week starting March 15, 2020 and run continuously until the week starting February 27, 2022.
source: For all provinces, model-inference was initiated the week starting March 15, 2020 and run continuously until the week starting February 27, 2022.
evidence: This describes the temporal scope of the model-inference analysis.

claim: The model-inference process was repeated 100 times for each province, each with 500 model realizations, totaling 50,000 model estimates.
source: To account for model stochasticity, we repeated the model-inference process 100 times for each province, each with 500 model realizations and summarized the results from all 50,000 model estimates.
evidence: This describes the approach to quantifying uncertainty in the model estimates.

claim: High prior immunity does not preclude new outbreaks, as neither infection nor current vaccination is sterilizing.
source: First, high prior immunity does not preclude new outbreaks, as neither infection nor current vaccination is sterilizing.
evidence: This is a general observation drawn from the findings in South Africa and supported by the data showing repeated waves despite high infection rates.

claim: Large numbers of hospitalizations and/or deaths can still occur in later waves with large infection surges, even though prior infection may provide partial protection.
source: Second, large numbers of hospitalizations and/or deaths can still occur in later waves with large infection surges, even though prior infection may provide partial protection and to some extent temper disease severity.
evidence: This is a general observation supported by the data from the Delta wave in South Africa.

claim: Variants capable of eroding a wide spectrum of prior immunity would have a greater chance of causing new major outbreaks.
source: Nonetheless, given high exposure and vaccination in many populations, variants capable of eroding a wide spectrum of prior immunity (i.e. from infection by multiple preexisting variants and vaccination) would have a greater chance of causing new major outbreaks.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed patterns of variant emergence and spread.
